name: THE GUAC! OR MY MOM WILL SHOOT BURGER

recipe.history:
Guacamole traces its origins to the Aztec civilization of central Mexico, where the avocado — known in Nahuatl as 'ahuacatl' — was cultivated and consumed as a sacred food believed to confer strength and fertility. The Aztec preparation, 'ahuacamolli,' combined mashed avocado with tomato, chili, and salt, creating a primitive form of what we recognize today. Spanish conquistadors encountering the dish in the 16th century were alternately fascinated and revolted by its green, fatty richness, so unlike anything in the European culinary vocabulary. They brought avocados back to Spain, and from there the fruit spread slowly through the Caribbean, Central America, and eventually into Californian and Texan cuisine through the Spanish mission system. The avocado's fat composition — over 70 percent monounsaturated oleic acid — made it a caloric powerhouse for indigenous people in a landscape where calories could be scarce, and this same fat is precisely what makes guacamole so endlessly satisfying.

Guacamole became an American obsession through the Mexican-American communities of the Southwest, particularly in California and Texas, where avocado cultivation expanded dramatically in the 20th century. The Hass avocado, developed in California in the 1920s and 1930s, democratized the fruit — hardier, richer, and with a longer shelf life than older varieties, it made guacamole available year-round across the country. By the 1980s and 1990s, guacamole was a fixture at Super Bowl parties and casual restaurants, and the logic of putting it on a burger was irresistible: its creaminess could replace mayo, its brightness replaced raw acidity, and its green color contrasted beautifully with the dark sear of beef. The California burger — with avocado or guacamole, often with bacon and Swiss — became one of the defining regional burger styles of the late 20th century.

My relationship with guacamole is personal in the way that only truly simple foods can be. I was taught to make it by my college roommate's mother during a Thanksgiving visit when I was nineteen, standing in a kitchen in Oxnard while she explained that the only equipment you need is a fork and the only skill you need is restraint. She mashed the avocado loosely — 'you want chunks, not baby food' — and added lime juice, white onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and salt, tasted it twice, adjusted the salt once, and declared it done in under five minutes. I have made it thousands of times since and I have never materially improved on what she taught me that afternoon. Good guacamole is not a recipe. It is a philosophy of leaving things alone.

A burger cooked to medium rare, 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, is the only canvas worthy of guacamole. The avocado's fat — silky, cool, herbaceous — requires a counterpart that is equally rich, and a properly medium rare patty provides exactly that: rendered beef fat, pink and juicy, a deep mineral sear on the crust, a yielding interior. Guacamole laid over a well-done burger is a mismatch of textures and temperatures, the avocado's creaminess amplifying the dryness of overcooked beef in the worst possible way. Medium rare keeps the beef alive and the guacamole in conversation with it. Cook to 130 to 135. Taste the guacamole. Trust yourself.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 medium Roma tomato, seeded and diced
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with the dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.
2. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
3. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and let proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C).
4. Brush with egg wash, sprinkle sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool completely on a wire rack before slicing.
5. Cook the bacon: In a cold skillet, lay bacon strips flat. Heat over medium, turning occasionally, until crispy and deeply browned, about 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer to paper towels. Reserve skillet.

6. Make the guacamole: Halve and pit the avocados. Scoop flesh into a bowl. Add lime juice immediately to prevent browning. Using a fork, mash to a chunky consistency — some large pieces are desirable. Fold in white onion, jalapeño, cilantro, garlic, and Roma tomato. Season with salt. Taste and adjust lime and salt. Cover tightly with plastic wrap pressed directly onto the surface and refrigerate until assembly.

7. Shape patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions. Combine salt, pepper, cumin, and smoked paprika and season patties on both sides. Shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple in the center of each.
8. Heat the reserved bacon skillet over high heat until the remaining bacon fat shimmers and begins to smoke. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes.

9. Flip patties, place a slice of pepper jack cheese on each, and cook 2 to 3 more minutes, checking temperature. Remove from heat at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
10. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

11. Assemble: Spread a thick layer of guacamole on the bottom bun. Add a leaf of green leaf lettuce, then the patty with melted pepper jack. Lay two strips of bacon over the cheese. Spoon additional guacamole on top. Close the bun and serve with a lime wedge on the side.
